p.title: Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization

ext.title: Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization
ext.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, vol. 42, pp. 427-486 (2011); extended version of a Conference on Learning Theory 2010 paper (pp. 333-345). Text copy is arXiv:1003.3967v5 [cs.LG], revised 6 Dec 2017.
ext.document_type: Journal article (theoretical computer science / AI; approximation-guarantee paper with applications and a small experimental section)
ext.coverage: Read the entire extracted text file (4,038 lines, 200,087 chars) in chunks: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-14 (pp. 1-36), references (pp. 37-41), and Appendix 15 (pp. 41-60, all proofs including costs, Theorems 38-40, Lemmas 36-51, and the Theorem 26 hardness proof). Figures 1-6 are read only through their extracted captions and axis text; numeric values plotted in Figure 5 are not in the text layer. Metadata hint corrected: the venue is JAIR 42 (2011), not just the arXiv number; the copyright line reads 2012. Paul's markup: no annotation file keyed to this document exists in research\_annots or research\annotations, so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Can the diminishing-returns property of classical submodular set functions be generalized to adaptive policies, so that a simple adaptive greedy policy is near-optimal for partially observable stochastic maximization, minimum-cost coverage and min-sum cover problems, with applications to sensor placement, stochastic set cover, viral marketing and active learning?
ext.theory: Adaptive submodularity (Definition 3, Eq. 11, p. 8): for partial realizations psi subset psi', the conditional expected marginal benefit Delta(e|psi) of any fixed item e must satisfy Delta(e|psi) >= Delta(e|psi'). It is defined relative to a known prior distribution p(phi) over realizations, and reduces to classical submodularity when the prior is deterministic (p. 6-7). Adaptive monotonicity (Definition 2, p. 8) is nonnegativity of Delta(e|psi). Strong adaptive monotonicity and strong adaptive submodularity (Definitions 10 and 12, pp. 13-14) are stronger conditions needed for the average-cost bounds. Pointwise submodularity plus adaptive submodularity implies strong adaptive submodularity (Lemma 39, p. 45). The authors show pointwise submodularity alone does not imply adaptive submodularity (counterexample, p. 14).
ext.data: Theoretical core: no empirical sample. Items are ground-set elements (e.g., sensor locations, graph nodes, unlabeled examples or hypotheses) with a Bayesian prior over realizations. Experiments (Section 10, pp. 29-32): (a) Intel Research Berkeley temperature data, 46 sensors, sampled every 30 seconds for 5 consecutive days starting 28 Feb 2004, covariance estimated empirically; (b) traffic speed data from 357 sensors on I-880 South, California, working days 6 AM-11 AM for one month. Unit of analysis: sensor location (item) and realization. The Figure 5 experiments use a 50% (p_fail = 0.5) failure rate; the lazy-evaluation curves are averaged over 100 runs (temperature) and 10 runs (traffic) per Figure 5 captions.
ext.method: Formal analysis: define policies over partial realizations, define adaptive monotonicity and submodularity, prove greedy guarantees by a Nemhauser-style argument extended to adaptive policies (Theorem 5 with a lemma on budgeted policies), average- and worst-case cover bounds via a charging/integration argument (Theorems 13-14, Lemma 47), a min-sum bound via a geometric argument of Feige et al. (2004) (Theorem 15), data-dependent upper bounds via a greedy linear program (Lemma 6, Lemma 37, Algorithm 3), a lazy/accelerated greedy (Algorithm 2), application reductions (Sections 6-9), a gap construction (Theorem 25), and a hardness reduction from a permanent-based puzzle (Feige and Lund 1997) with treasure-hunting instances (Theorem 26). Empirical part: Gaussian-process entropy objective I(X_V; Y_A) for sensor selection with failure probability, comparing naive vs. lazy adaptive greedy by wall-clock time and count of objective evaluations, and comparing the data-dependent bounds beta_avg to the greedy reward.
ext.identification: Not applicable. This is a theoretical approximation-guarantee paper; no causal identification strategy. Guarantees are conditional on the adaptive submodularity property holding with respect to the stated (known) prior p(phi), and on complexity-theoretic assumptions for the hardness results.
ext.scope: Scope is the class of adaptive stochastic optimization problems over finite item sets with known priors (sensor placement with unreliable sensors; stochastic set cover; adaptive influence/viral marketing under the independent cascade model with full-adoption feedback; pool-based active learning and generalized binary search; optimal decision trees). No human population, institution, legislature, election, lobbying, or text corpus is studied. Era: conference version 2010, journal 2011, arXiv revision 2017.

key_findings.finding: Adaptive greedy policy with budget k achieves at least (1 - 1/e) of the value of the best adaptive policy for adaptive monotone submodular objectives; an alpha-approximate greedy policy achieves (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) when run for l steps.
Adaptive submodularity generalizes classical submodularity; for deterministic priors it reduces to the classical notion, and the greedy guarantee of Nemhauser et al. (1978) carries over.

Average-cost minimum cover: greedy policy costs at most alpha * cavg(opt) * (ln(Q/(delta*eta)) + 1)^2 in general instances, and alpha * cavg(opt) * (ln(Q/eta) + 1)^2 for self-certifying instances. Worst-case cost bound (Theorem 14) is alpha * cwc(opt) * (ln(Q/(delta*eta)) + 1), with the self-certifying worst-case log bound left open.
key_findings.location: Theorem 13, Section 5.2.1, p. 14; Theorem 14, Section 5.2.2, p. 14; Discussion Section 5.2.3, p. 15
key_findings.numbers: squared-log factor for average cost; single-log factor for worst cost; delta = min prior probability; eta = coverage gap

key_findings.finding: Historical correction: an earlier version claimed logarithmic (not squared-logarithmic) average-cost factors; the authors say the proof was flawed, as pointed out by Nan and Saligrama (2017). Whether the log bounds hold, and whether strong adaptive submodularity is required, are open.

Feige's (1998) Set Cover hardness implies no polynomial-time (1 - epsilon) ln(Q/eta) approximation for self-certifying Adaptive Stochastic Min Cost Cover, and no (1 - epsilon) ln(Q/(delta*eta)) approximation for general instances, under NP not in DTIME(n^{O(log log n)}); the worst-case self-certifying log bound remains open.
Adaptive min-sum cover: greedy policy is a 4 alpha approximation to the min-sum cost (Adaptive Stochastic Min-Sum Cover), extending Feige, Lovasz and Tetali (2004) and Streeter and Golovin (2008).
key_findings.location: Theorem 15, Section 5.3.2, p. 16; proof Section 15.5, pp. 56-57

key_findings.finding: Stochastic submodular maximization with multiple failure types (generalizing Asadpour et al. 2008 all-or-nothing failures): the greedy policy obtains (1 - 1/e) of the best adaptive policy when sensor states are independent and the utility is monotone submodular.

Stochastic set cover with arbitrary per-item set distributions and independent sampling: the adaptive greedy algorithm is a (ln n + 1)^2 approximation, where n = |U|, improving on Liu et al. (2008) H_n for two-state items.
key_findings.location: Corollary 18, Section 7.1, p. 19; Liu et al. comparison p. 19

key_findings.finding: Adaptive viral marketing under the independent cascade model with full-adoption feedback is adaptive submodular for any monotone submodular reward, so greedy seeding achieves 1 - 1/e of the best adaptive policy; a minimum-cost cover version has a (ln(Q/eta)+1)^2 guarantee.
key_findings.location: Theorem 19, Section 8.2, p. 21 (proof pp. 21-23); Theorem 20, Section 8.3, p. 23

key_findings.finding: The authors retract an earlier claim that viral marketing is adaptive submodular under the myopic feedback model, giving a 3-node counterexample (edges u->v with p=1 and v->w with p=1-epsilon); they conjecture a constant-factor greedy guarantee still holds there.
key_findings.location: Section 8.2.1 'A Comment on the Myopic Feedback Model', p. 23
key_findings.numbers: p_uv = 1, p_vw = 1 - epsilon; Delta(w|psi) = epsilon < 1 = Delta(w|psi')

key_findings.finding: Generalized binary search (GBS) for pool-based active learning with a Bayesian prior: expected number of queries is at most OPT * (ln(1/min_h p_H(h)) + 1)^2; with a uniform prior, OPT * (ln(|H|-1)+1)^2; with the modified prior p'(h) proportional to max(p_H(h), 1/|H|^2) the factor becomes O((ln|H|)^2).
key_findings.location: Theorem 21, Section 9, p. 25; uniform prior Section 9.2, p. 26; arbitrary priors Section 9.3, p. 27; highly nonuniform priors Section 9.4, p. 28

key_findings.finding: Gupta et al. (2010) achieve O(log|H|) for active learning / optimal decision trees with non-uniform costs and general priors using a non-greedy algorithm; the paper states this removes the cost and probability dependence from the bound.

Lazy (accelerated) adaptive greedy gives large speedups without loss of solution quality on sensor selection with unreliable sensors, because submodularity lets stale marginal gains serve as upper bounds.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, p. 9 (intro summary: roughly 4 to 40 times); Section 10.1.2, pp. 30-31
key_findings.numbers: temperature data (46 sensors): roughly 3.5-7x fewer evaluations/time; traffic data (357 sensors): 30-38x

key_findings.finding: Data-dependent upper bounds beta_avg (average of k+1 bounds along the realized trajectory) are tighter than the worst-case guarantee in the sensor experiments; lazy-bound versions are almost as tight as eager versions with slightly higher variance.
key_findings.location: Section 10.1.3, pp. 31-32; Lemma 6, Eq. 13, p. 11; Figures 5(e)-(f) p. 32
key_findings.numbers: bounds 'tighter than the worst case bounds' (no numeric values given in text layer)

key_findings.finding: Adaptivity gap: for adaptive submodular objectives, the adaptivity gap of Adaptive Stochastic Min-Sum Cover (and of min-cost cover in that instance) is Omega(n / log n), while for Stochastic Set Coverage without multiplicities it is Omega(|E|) (Goemans and Vondrak 2006); for Max-Coverage Asadpour et al. show a 1 - 1/e gap.

Hardness without adaptive submodularity: unless PH = Sigma_2^P, no polynomial-time algorithm approximates Adaptive Stochastic Maximization, Min Cost Coverage, or Min-Sum Cover within O(|E|^{1-epsilon}), even for pointwise modular objectives.
key_findings.location: Theorem 26, Section 12, p. 33 (proof Section 15.7, pp. 57-60); Corollaries 27-28, p. 34

key_findings.finding: Pointwise submodularity alone is not sufficient for adaptive submodularity; counterexample with f(S, phi) = |{e in S: phi(e)=1}| and a two-point prior gives Delta(e|empty) = 1/2 but Delta(e|{(e',1)}) = 1.
key_findings.location: Section 3.2 after Definition 12, p. 14 (text reads on p. 14 lines 733-736)

limitations: Guarantees hold only for objectives that satisfy adaptive submodularity with respect to a known prior p(phi); the property is distribution-dependent (p. 8), and the authors note an objective can be adaptive submodular under one prior but not another.
The prior is assumed known (footnote 2, p. 4). Robustness to prior error is shown only for multiplicative error alpha = d/c (Section 4.3, p. 9).
Item selection is assumed not to alter the realization, so general POMDPs with action-dependent state changes are outside the framework (Section 3.4, p. 9; Section 13.7, p. 36).
Treasure-hunting-type instances with strong synergies between items are not covered (Section 3.4, p. 9; Theorem 26, p. 33).
The average-cost bounds carry squared-logarithmic factors; the authors say the logarithmic version is open, and that the earlier log-factor proof was flawed (Historical Note, p. 14).
Open: whether strong adaptive submodularity is required for Theorem 13 (p. 14); whether the worst-case self-certifying log bound holds (p. 15).
Myopic-feedback influence model: adaptive submodularity was retracted and only a constant-factor greedy guarantee is conjectured (p. 23).
Greedy guarantees assume exact or alpha-approximate greedy selection; sampled marginal gains give only additive error bounds (Section 5.1, p. 11).
Hardness results rest on complexity assumptions (PH = Sigma_2^P, NP not in DTIME(n^{O(log log n)})), and the Gupta et al. O(log|H|) result is cited rather than proven here (p. 29).

Experiments are limited to two sensor datasets (46-sensor Berkeley temperature; 357-sensor I-880 traffic), with failure probability 0.5 in the reported runs; no statistical tests and no social-network or real-diffusion data are used. The viral-marketing and active-learning applications are analytic, not empirical.
The paper treats uniform-cost items in the main text; cost-sensitive results are deferred to the appendix (Section 2.4, p. 6; Appendix 15).
measures: Average cost cavg(pi) = expected number of items selected
Worst-case cost cwc(pi) = max over realizations of items selected
Min-sum cost c_Sigma(pi) = sum over t of (E[f(E,Phi)] - favg(pi[<t]))
Conditional expected marginal benefit Delta(e|psi) and policy benefit Delta(pi|psi)
Coverage quota Q and coverage gap eta; minimum prior probability delta = min p(phi)
Mutual information I(X_V; Y_A) = H(X_V) - H(X_V|Y_A) used as the sensor-selection objective
Wall-clock time and number of objective-function evaluations (naive vs. lazy adaptive greedy)
Data-dependent upper bound beta_avg on the optimal expected reward
Version-space prior mass in active learning (GBS), and number of queries in expectation
Adaptivity gap (ratio of optimal non-adaptive to optimal adaptive expected cost)
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg and Tardos (2003), Maximizing the spread of influence through a social network, KDD: independent cascade model; expected spread is submodular. Base for the adaptive viral-marketing section.
Leskovec et al. (2007), Cost-effective outbreak detection in networks, KDD: lazy evaluations and data-dependent bounds for non-adaptive submodular selection.
Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher (1978): greedy (1 - 1/e) guarantee for monotone submodular maximization; the template for Theorem 5.
Wolsey (1982) and Feige (1998): greedy submodular cover bounds and the matching Set Cover hardness.
Krause and Guestrin (2005, 2007, 2009a): mutual-information sensor placement; source of the submodularity of I(X_V; Y_A) used in Section 10.
Asadpour, Nazerzadeh and Saberi (2008), Stochastic submodular maximization: (1 - 1/e) for all-or-nothing sensor failures; generalized here.
Goemans and Vondrak (2006), Stochastic covering and adaptivity: stochastic set cover and adaptivity gaps.
Liu et al. (2008), Near-optimal algorithms for shared filter evaluation in data stream systems: H_n approximation for two-state stochastic set cover.
Golovin, Krause and Ray (2010), Near-optimal Bayesian active learning with noisy observations, and Bellala and Scott (2010): squared-log bounds for persistent noise.
Guillory and Bilmes (2010, 2011), Interactive submodular set cover and noisy variant: worst-case logarithmic bounds; differing setup.
Gupta, Krishnaswamy, Nagarajan and Ravi (2010), Approximation algorithms for optimal decision trees and adaptive TSP: O(log|H|) for active learning with costs.
Nan and Saligrama (2017), comments on the proof of adaptive stochastic set cover: identified the flaw in the earlier log-factor claim.
Feige, Lovasz and Tetali (2004), Approximating min sum set cover: the geometric argument behind the 4-approximation in Theorem 15.
Dasgupta (2004) and Kosaraju, Przytycka and Borgstrom (1999): greedy GBS guarantees and the modified prior p'(h).
Golovin and Krause (2011b), Adaptive submodular optimization under matroid constraints: follow-on work covering matroid and p-independence constraints (Section 13.8, p. 35).

short_quotes.quote: a simple adaptive greedy algorithm is guaranteed to be competitive with the optimal policy

rel.summary_md:
Golovin and Krause extend the diminishing-returns idea behind submodular set functions to adaptive policies. In their setting you pick an item, observe its random outcome, then pick the next item. If the objective's conditional expected marginal gain never rises as more is observed (adaptive submodularity, which is defined relative to a known prior), then adaptive greedy gets at least (1-1/e) of the best adaptive policy. The paper also gives squared-log bounds for minimum-cost cover, a 4-approximation for min-sum cover, data-dependent upper bounds (Lemma 6), and a lazy greedy variant (Algorithm 2) that ran about 3.5-7x faster on 46 sensors and 30-38x faster on 357 sensors. Its limits matter as much as its results. The prior must be known. Sampled marginal gains carry only additive error bounds. The myopic-feedback influence model was retracted. Without adaptive submodularity, Theorem 26 rules out any polynomial-time approximation within O(|E|^(1-eps)).

For Melange, the paper mainly sets the scope of the allocation tier's guarantees. The joint optimizer (fec/engine/optimize.py) uses lazy greedy and a G-K data-dependent bound. It correctly states that it is not an adaptive policy: `observations` is empty, and modeled threshold conversions void the certificate. In its fixed-state case, the separable concave structure gives an exact grid optimum, which is stronger than (1-1/e). The budget frontier, the coalition allocator and the dashboard's budgetRecruit are a different matter. Each claims or implies submodular guarantees that this paper does not supply, because of MC=20 sampled marginals, a competitive two-colour kernel, per-candidate fac or target-distance weights, and singleton-marginal water-fill. The seed gate's independent per-seed take-up matches the structure of the paper's Theorem 16. None of these systems observes real outcomes, so the adaptive half of the paper is not built. All of this analysis is UNVERIFIED (DE-062): one reading of the code, with no second path.

bearings.paper_claim: Lazy greedy (Algorithm 2) loses no quality because stale marginals upper-bound current ones under submodularity: about 3.5-7x fewer evaluations on 46 sensors and 30-38x on 357 sensors (failure rate 0.5). The data-dependent bound (sum of the top-k current marginals over the current value) bounds the optimum and was tighter than the worst-case (1-1/e) bound in the sensor runs.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.4 p. 9; Algorithm 2; Lemma 6 / Eq. 13 p. 11; Lemma 37 (appendix); Section 10.1.2-10.1.3 pp. 30-32
bearings.system_side: A heap-based lazy greedy over $500 chunks re-queues a member only when its marginal is stale. dd_bound fills the budget with each member's current next-chunk marginal multiplied by its remaining PMAX headroom. It is reported only under a fixed-state concavity certificate, and the code labels exact greedy optimality as stronger than the (1-1/e) floor.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This carries over in the deterministic fixed-stance case. Per-member concave chunk sequences let headroom-times-current-marginal stand in for top-k items, as concavity_violations() checks. In that case the bound is a valid upper bound but only a diagnostic, because greedy is already exact. It does not carry over once modeled conversions fire. The code's citation 'Lemma 5.3 / A.9' does not match the numbering in the vault's arXiv v5 copy (Lemma 6, Lemma 37).

bearings.paper_claim: Theorem 5's (1-1/e) guarantee is relative to the best adaptive policy only if item outcomes are observed and the objective is adaptive monotone submodular under a known prior p(phi). Items with strong synergies (treasure-hunting instances) fall outside the class. Without the property, Theorem 26 gives no O(|E|^(1-eps)) approximation unless PH = Sigma_2^P.
bearings.paper_location: Definitions 2-3 p. 8; Theorem 5 p. 11; Section 3.4 p. 9; Theorem 26 p. 33
bearings.system_side: Nothing is observed (`observations=[]`). When cumulative CU dollars cross the deterministic DTHRESH defection threshold, the member is banked as won, the stance matrix shifts, and the queue is rebuilt. The run is then labelled modeled_threshold_replanning with guarantee kind 'none'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the code's refusal to claim a certificate in conversion mode. A threshold jump makes a chunk's marginal rise after earlier chunks, which is the synergy that breaks adaptive submodularity. The bearing would change only if real post-contribution outcomes were observed and a prior over member responses were specified, and neither exists.

bearings.paper_claim: Stochastic submodular maximization: with independent item states (multiple failure types) and a monotone submodular utility, greedy gets (1-1/e) of the best adaptive policy (generalizing Asadpour et al. 2008). Robustness to a misspecified prior is shown only for multiplicative error alpha = d/c.
bearings.paper_location: Theorem 16, Section 6 p. 17; Section 4.3 p. 9; footnote 2 p. 4
bearings.system_side: Each lobbied seed activates independently with probability gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob x SGATE[tier]). Draws come from a dedicated per-node CRN key range (2^62 offset). SGATE runs from 1.00 (Highly Persuadable) down to 0.35 (Opponent), all design constants.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The structure matches: independent per-seed Bernoulli take-up over a spread function. The guarantee carries over only if spread given the activated seeds is monotone submodular, which is not shown for this competitive kernel, and only if the take-up probabilities are known. SGATE and seed_prob are unestimated, and H1 is unscored (F5 underpowered, 72 of 511 new-event members), so the 'known prior' assumption fails. The paper's robustness result covers only a bounded multiplicative error.

bearings.paper_claim: Greedy guarantees assume exact or alpha-approximate marginal evaluation. Marginal gains estimated by sampling give only additive error bounds. The adaptive IC result (Theorem 19) covers a single cascade with full-adoption feedback, and the myopic-feedback version was retracted with a 3-node counterexample.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.1 p. 11; Theorem 19 p. 21; Section 8.2.1 p. 23
bearings.system_side: Lazy greedy picks up to 60 seeds. Each marginal is a 20-draw CRN Monte Carlo estimate (MC=20) over a two-colour first-to-reach cascade with money-mobilized bystanders. Marginals are clamped at max(0, .) and multiplied by a per-candidate factor fac (REPFAC x lev or c) before ranking. The knee is read from the noisy raw path.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No G-K guarantee carries over as built. Marginals are sampled (additive error at 20 draws), the selection score is fac-weighted rather than the reported spread, and the objective is a competitive kernel this paper does not cover. The negative-marginal clamp signals that sampled spread is not monotone. The frontier is a non-adaptive heuristic. Its 'diminishing returns' assumption is empirical, not certified.

bearings.paper_claim: Near-optimality comes from greedy selection that conditions each pick on what has already been selected or observed. For deterministic priors the notion reduces to classical submodularity, and Nemhauser et al.'s greedy (1-1/e) applies.
bearings.paper_location: Sections 3.1-3.2 pp. 6-8; Theorem 5 p. 11; Conclusions p. 36
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator ranks the top-45 neutral candidates by singleton marginals spread({n}) - base. It splits $2M across them pro rata by water-fill with a $50k cap, with no sequential greedy conditioning, then reports the honest joint spread. A comment asserts 'spread is submodular'. The flip allocator is an exact greedy over saturating pflip chunks.
bearings.transfer_conditions: For the flip allocator, a fixed-state separable concave pflip makes greedy exact, so the paper adds nothing. For the coalition allocator, singleton-marginal proportional split is not greedy, so no submodular guarantee applies even if spread were submodular. Reporting joint versus naive-additive spread is the right diagnostic. The submodularity assertion is unverified for the bystander-filtered competitive kernel.

bearings.paper_claim: The (1-1/e) greedy guarantee holds for the monotone submodular objective that greedy actually maximizes. For deterministic outcomes the adaptive framework reduces to Nemhauser et al. Under IC with full-adoption feedback, observing which asks succeed keeps adaptive submodularity (Theorem 19).
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit maximizes probabilistic coverage cov[v] = 1 - prod(1 - p), which is submodular. But each candidate's marginal gain g is multiplied by (1 + 2 dT[c]) when a target is set, and the comment still claims the (1-1/e) guarantee for the reported reach. No ask outcome is observed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Without a target (dT null), the classical guarantee holds for reach. With a target, the selection score is not the marginal gain of any fixed submodular function, so the (1-1/e) comment overstates the claim. The adaptive version would need recruit outcomes fed back into the dashboard, which is not built.

gaps_exposed: No adaptive loop. No allocator observes real outcomes, such as cosponsorship or vote movement after a contribution or ask, and conditions later picks on them. optimize.py reserves `observations=[]` but never fills it, so the adaptive half of Golovin and Krause (Theorem 5 relative to the best adaptive policy) is unavailable.

No explicit prior over member responses. The adaptive guarantees require a known p(phi). SGATE, seed_prob, DTHRESH and PERS are owner constants with no calibrated distribution, and the prospective H1/H2 contract that could estimate them is unscored (F5 underpowered).

Sampled marginals carry no error control. The frontier and coalition engines rank on MC=20 estimates, while the paper gives only additive-error guarantees for sampled greedy. No MC-size-to-error-bound link is computed beyond the top-k stability check.

Submodularity of the competitive cascade objective is asserted, not tested. That covers the two-colour first-to-reach race with money bystanders filtered by `n not in s` and an order-dependent tie-break. No numeric diminishing-returns probe like optimize.py's concavity_violations() exists for spread().

The adaptivity gap is never measured. Theorem 25 shows adaptive versus non-adaptive cost can differ by Omega(n/log n) in cover problems. The system never estimates how much sequential re-targeting on observed outcomes would be worth.

Min-cost cover versions are not built. A question like 'cheapest set of asks to reach a quota of Q cosponsors' would fall under Theorems 13-14 (squared-log bounds), but only budget-maximization modes exist.
flags: Citation numbering: optimize.py:108 cites 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9' for the data-dependent bound. The vault's arXiv v5 copy numbers it Lemma 6 (Eq. 13), with appendix proof Lemma 37. Check against the JAIR print before quoting.

Overstated guarantee claim: the comment at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:775-776 claims (1-1/e) for budgetRecruit, but the target mode multiplies each candidate's marginal by (1 + 2 dT[c]), so the selected set is not certified for the reported reach.

Unverified submodularity assertions: per_topic_coalition.py:122 and scenario.py:10-11 state the coalition spread is submodular, citing Bharathi-Kempe-Salek. Golovin and Krause cover only single-cascade IC (Theorem 19). The implemented kernel adds money-mobilized bystanders filtered against the seed set, an order-dependent first-to-reach tie-break, and a fac weighting in the frontier, none of which this paper licenses.

Retracted model warning: if any future adaptive recruitment observes only immediate-neighbour responses (myopic feedback), Golovin and Krause retracted adaptive submodularity for that model (p. 23). It must not be cited as covered.

Paul's margin note on Chen 2023 (pressure from high-ranking members 'not diminishing') describes increasing marginal returns. That would put such pressure outside the adaptive-submodular class and under the Theorem 26 hardness result. Any model encoding it should drop the (1-1/e) language.

All bearings are a single-path agent reading of the code and remain UNVERIFIED per DE-062. No conflict was found with D-021, D-025, the two rejected SNA proposals, or the D-104..D-108 reciprocity status.
rel.paul_alignment: Partly aligned, and Paul's note is stale on one word: "adaptive". He calls adaptive greedy plus CELF the operational layer. The built joint optimizer does match the CELF half: lazy greedy, plus the G-K data-dependent bound as a diagnostic. In its fixed-state case it is stronger than greedy, because the separable concave objective makes greedy exactly optimal. It is not adaptive in Golovin and Krause's sense. Nothing real is observed, `observations` is empty, and the code itself says replanning after a modeled threshold conversion is not an adaptive policy and voids the certificate. So the paper underwrites the guarantee language only for the fixed-state optimizer. The frontier, coalition and dashboard recruitment heuristics fall outside it as built: sampled MC=20 marginals, weighted selection scores, a competitive kernel, and a singleton-marginal split. Paul expects GCOMB to replace greedy at scale, but this paper gives no reason to: at 533 members, lazy greedy is cheap and exact where it applies. Paul's per-topic-allocators position places these in the 'static and submodular tier', but submodularity is assumed there, not checked. His Chen 2023 note on non-diminishing pressure points the same way, toward objectives outside this paper's class.

related.why: This is the COLT 2010 conference version. The JAIR/arXiv v5 text extends it with costs, the min-sum cover result and the hardness proofs. It also corrects the earlier logarithmic average-cost claim to squared-log and retracts the myopic-feedback viral-marketing claim.

Contingency-aware seeding, where a lobbied seed takes up with some probability, is the setting of Theorem 16's independent item states. Chen et al. learn the policy by RL, where Golovin and Krause prove greedy guarantees. The seed gate implements Chen's idea.

Golovin and Krause cover single-cascade IC only. Bharathi et al. supply the follower-submodularity result that scenario.py relies on for the coalition (1-1/e) claim, and its tie-break assumptions decide whether that claim holds for the built kernel.

Shows that competitive threshold models can be non-submodular, which puts the flip/LT side in the Theorem 26 territory where greedy has no guarantee. scenario.py cites both papers for this scope split.

Under complex contagion, marginal gains can increase, which violates adaptive submodularity. That is why Chen et al. turn to RL instead of adaptive greedy. Paul's own note links this to non-diminishing pressure.
RELINK's closed-network IM is non-submodular, so Golovin and Krause's guarantees do not apply. The dashboard's closedCascadeRoute correctly disclaims (1-1/e) on this basis.
Learns sampling policies when the network or prior is unknown. That addresses the known-prior assumption (footnote 2) that Melange's unestimated SGATE and seed_prob constants violate.

Benchmarks heuristic centrality against greedy IM. It is relevant to whether the dashboard's PageRank prior or the greedy guarantee should carry the weight, given that Golovin and Krause's guarantee needs exact or alpha-approximate marginals.

paul_entries.text:
**Golovin, D., & Krause, A. (2011).** *Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization.* Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 42, 427–486. arXiv:1003.3967. https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.3967

The single most load-bearing reference for the operational layer. Generalizes submodular set functions to *adaptive policies* — choose, observe the outcome, choose again — and proves that under adaptive submodularity a simple adaptive-greedy policy is competitive with the optimal policy, inheriting the classic (1 − 1/e) guarantee. Critically, the authors were the first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model, selecting seeds sequentially with each choice made after observing the spread of prior ones. This is the formal IM analog of D* Lite's incremental replanning: a greedy routine that re-optimizes as intelligence arrives, with a provable bound. The practical caveat — and the reason one still drifts toward learned methods — is that it presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard to compute in general.
